---
title: "How Fast Does Normal Happen?"
subtitle: "Stress-testing the Central Limit Theorem with Monte Carlo simulation"
---

This repository investigates how quickly the sampling distribution of the sample
mean becomes approximately normal. The analysis compares symmetric, skewed,
discrete, heavy-tailed, dependent, non-identically distributed, and mixture
populations.

## Research question

> What is the smallest sample size at which the sampling distribution of the
> sample mean is reasonably defensible as approximately normal?

There is no universal answer. This project uses the same diagnostic standard
for every population, then explains where that standard works and where the
usual Central Limit Theorem assumptions fail.

## Answer in brief

The answer is ambiguous because “approximately normal” is a judgment based on
the population being averaged, the diagnostic thresholds, the sample sizes
investigated, Monte Carlo variation, and the assumptions behind the CLT. It is
not a universal switch that turns on at (n=30).

Using `B = 10000`, the current seed `6599`, and the same four diagnostics for
every population, the first stable passing values were:

| Population | First stable passing (n) |
|---|---:|
| Standard normal | 2 |
| Continuous uniform | 5 |
| Symmetric binomial | 5 |
| Six-sided die | 10 |
| Poisson | 30 |
| Rare-success binomial | 50 |
| Two-component mixture | 50 |
| Non-identical Bernoulli | 75 |
| Exponential | 100 |
| Dependent process | None through 500 |
| Cauchy | None through 500 |

For example, the Poisson population passed at (n=30) with skewness about
0.142, while the Exponential population still had skewness about 0.398 at
(n=30) and did not pass until (n=100). The Cauchy population failed even at
(n=500), where its simulated skewness was about 87.46 and excess kurtosis was
about 8213.51.

Therefore, the defensible answer is population-specific: select the smallest
sample size whose graphical and numerical evidence meets a clearly stated
standard. In this project, the answer ranges from (n=2) to (n=100) for the
finite-variance independent populations, while the dependent and Cauchy cases
do not meet the standard within the investigated range.

## How to read the project

- Read the individual population analyses for the simulations and evidence.
- Read the [final summary](final-summary.qmd) for the cross-distribution comparison.
- See `R/helpers.R` for the shared simulation and diagnostic definitions.
- See `ai-log.md` for the record of prompts, validation, and revisions.

## Reproducibility

The analyses use base R and a single student seed. Replace `student_id <- 6599`
in each analysis with the last four digits of your own student ID before
rendering. The Monte Carlo repetition count is `B = 10000`.
